• Other names: Bolbitis Mini, Creeping Fern, El Nino Fern, Asian Water Fern, African Water Fern
  • Difficulty: moderate
  • Lighting: low to moderate
  • Optimal pH: 6.0–7.0
  • Optimal GH: 1–10
  • Optimal temperature: 22–25°C (72–77°F)
  • Substrate: any
  • Can be grown emersed: yes
  • Growth rate: low
  • Placement in tank: foreground and midground
  • Aquarium size: 10–15 cm (4–6 inches)
  • Fertilizers: low requirements
  • CO2: low requirements
  • Propagation: rhizome division
  • Colour: green

Bolbitis heteroclita grows extremely slowly and is naturally a terrestrial plant. It has been listed in the Chinese traditional system as medicinal.

This species is widely distributed in the southern and southeastern Asian tropics. It is native to Assam, Bangladesh, Borneo, Caroline Is., China South-Central, China Southeast, Christmas I., East Himalaya, Hainan, Jawa, Malaya, Maluku, Myanmar, Nansei-shoto, Nepal, New Guinea, Philippines, Solomon Is., Sulawesi, Sumatera, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

In its natural habitat, Bolbitis heteroclita is commonly found in roadside areas within tropical Asia, at altitudes between 150 and 750 metres above sea level.

The plant is primarily terrestrial and thrives in shaded environments. It is often observed on rocks, at the base of trees, or near streams.

The species prefers mesophyte habitats, which are environments with moderate moisture levels. Its ability to adapt as a terrestrial shade plant or lithophyte enables it to colonize a variety of ecological niches within its range.

In nature it inhabits different soil types (red soil, loamy soil, laterite soil). It also climbs on tree trunks and thrives on rocks as well as along slopes.
If kept solely as an aquatic plant, it can even be suitable for nano aquariums. If grown in a semi-emergent state, it requires a larger aquarium, at least 80 litres (20 gallons).

Care depends on whether it is grown submerged or emersed.

Submersed form: closely monitor water parameters and avoid fluctuations, including temperature changes. Even under optimal conditions it grows extremely slowly; expect only a few leaves per month. Do regular water changes and avoid direct or intense light.

Emersed form: in a paludarium the plant is relatively resilient to changes, and its growth rate is moderate to high.

Planting: the leaves grow along the rhizome, so avoid burying the rhizome in the substrate as this can cause decay. Tie the plant to rocks or driftwood with cotton thread or fishing line, or use super glue or coral glue. To attach the rhizome: clean the surface of the driftwood or rock, apply a drop of glue, attach the rhizome and press it firmly. Keep the fern from drying out by maintaining adequate moisture.

Dry start method: the plant is grown without water at first. Instead of filling the tank after planting, add only enough water to reach the surface of the lowest part of the substrate. Make sure the leaves are above the water level from the start, placing the rhizome near the surface. Cover the top of the tank with cling wrap to increase humidity. After about 5 to 8 weeks you can flood the tank or turn it into a paludarium.

Propagation: in nature it propagates by growing little plants from the leaves (like Java fern). In aquariums it is usually propagated by rhizome division: carefully divide the plant with a sharp knife so that each piece has at least 3 leaflets, then attach the pieces to rocks or driftwood.

The ease of care depends on the growth form. Grown emergent or semi-emergent (e.g. in a paludarium) it is easy to maintain; kept fully submerged it can be challenging.

  • Temperature: 22–25°C (72–77°F). It does not tolerate cold or too warm water, or temperature fluctuations.
  • pH: slightly acidic to neutral (6.0–7.0). In alkaline water, leaf dissolution is often observed.
  • Hardness: ideally below 10 GH. In very hard water it often melts.
  • Flow: it does not like strong water flow.

Lighting: the plant is primarily terrestrial and thrives in shade, preferring reduced direct sunlight. In the aquatic environment, low to medium lighting is enough, and it can be good for low-tech tanks.

Substrate: the species can be terrestrial (growing in soil) or lithophytic (growing on rocks). A rocky substrate provides a good base for the fern to root upon.

CO2: a pressurized CO2 system is not mandatory. It may improve the growth rate but is completely optional.

Fertilization: the plant does fine without regular fertilizers, but it is still recommended to fertilize at least a few times a month.

If you plan to add it to a shrimp tank or a high-tech planted tank with CO2 and regular fertilization, note that a high level of CO2 and copper (most fertilizers contain copper) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Description: a terrestrial fern with elongated rhizomes and loosely placed leaves. It can be grown emersed or submersed. Leaves are thin and herbaceous; lateral pinnae are alternate, usually 1 to 4 pairs, with smooth or slightly serrated edges and a long, whip-like tip. The rhizome is about 10–15 mm thick and covered in scales. Leaves are bright green. Emersed plants reach up to 25 cm in height and about 15–17 cm in width; submersed leaves are about 10 cm long and 5 cm wide. Fertile leaflets are rarely formed. Varieties include Bolbitis heteroclita 'Asiatica', 'Difformis' and 'Cuspidata'.

Problems:

  • Melting: occurs if water parameters are unstable. Avoid drastic changes, keep lighting low to medium and the water clean.
  • Wilting: emergent plants submerged in water wilt because their leaves are not adapted. Trim the leaves to the base and wait for new submerged leaves to grow.
  • Turning black: leaves may blacken and the plant may die, which can be caused by hard water or planting the rhizome too deep.
  • Slow growth: it takes a long time to adapt to a new environment. Letting it grow emersed boosts its growth rate.

Tankmates: best kept with small, peaceful community fish that will not damage the plant, e.g. neon tetras, clown killifish, white cloud mountain minnows, zebra danio, cherry barb, platies, mollies, otocinclus and pygmy corydoras. For shrimp, choose species that prefer the same slightly acidic water, e.g. crystal red shrimp, blue bolt shrimp and Caridina cf. babaulti. Ornamental snails should not be kept long in low-pH water as it harms their shells, but if pH is close to 7.0 almost any snail or dwarf shrimp is possible.

Avoid: fish that may damage the plant or find it palatable, such as silver dollars, Buenos Aires tetras, koi, goldfish, oscars, rainbowfish, Jack Dempsey, clown loaches and African cichlids. Be careful with most crayfish and freshwater crabs, which cut, eat and uproot plants.

Bolbitis heteroclita is not fully aquatic and can be finicky, especially when fully submerged, so it is not suitable for beginners.
